To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

depression is associated with disturbances of neuroplasticty that are driven by reductions of neurotrophic factors and that the efficacy of antidepressants is at least partially related to their capacity to restore neuroplastic processes.

1) depression is a common and chronic disorder, 2) it is associated with aberrant neuroplastics, 3) these aberrations are likely driven by reductions of brain derived neurotropic factor (BDNF) and 4) the next wave of treatments for depression may target neuroplasticity and include ketamine and erythropoietic agents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiological underpinnings of depression, and the development of novel treatments that target neuroplasticity to improve the quality of life of those afflicted with this disorder.
the neurobiological mechanisms of depression and the development of novel antidepressants.
elucidating how neurotrophic and immune factors interact with genetic and environmental factors to promote depression and how these factors may be targeted to develop novel antidepressant strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the efficacy of antidepressants is at least partially related to their ability to promote neuroplasticity and that this mechanism may be the common denominator of all antidepressants, whether they are “traditional” or “next wave”.
depression is a complex disease with multiple contributing factors.
the next wave of treatments should be based on neuroplasticity and that these treatments should be used in combination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the neuroplasticity model of depression, which is consistent with the current DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for the disorder, can provide a useful framework for understanding depression pathophysiology and developing novel therapeutic interventions.
the next wave of treatments for depression will be those that modulate neuroplastics processes.
the future of antidepressant strategies is likely to be found in agents that promote neuroplasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
depression is a neuroplastic disorder, and that the next wave of depression treatments may be best targeted at restoring proper neuroplasticity.

neuroplasticity is a key target of current and “new” antidepressant strategies and that a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying such processes will lead to improved treatments for depression and related disorders.
the field of depression is ripe for the development of new and improved treatments based upon the concept of restoring neuroplasticity.
